en: Preface to the Revised Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra:
According to the records compiled by the ancestral masters of the Nanshan school, both monks and nuns possess revised versions of the *Prātimokṣa* (Precepts Text).

While the monastic version is currently in circulation throughout the world, the nun’s version has not yet spread to this region. What is currently recited here is merely a later compilation extracted from the Vinaya according to the standards of subsequent generations.
Furthermore, while these [scriptures] are prepared for practical use, because their translations favor a质朴 (zhūpò—plain and unadorned) style, they are especially difficult to receive and recite.

Consequently, there are those who do not even recite them after completing the initiation rite (*dītán*), or though they do practice recitation, few are able to see it through to the end. Thus, while those who receive [the teachings] are as numerous as the hair on an ox’s body, those who uphold them are as rare as a unicorn’s horn.

Internally harboring the essence of the Dharma yet externally wearing the robes of a Buddha, they instead mingle with the secular world to pursue livelihoods and indulge their passions in committing evil, thereby inviting retribution from others.

To revile and disparage me, to defile the stream of the Dharma for my disciples, to consume the offerings of the faithful in vain, to deviate from the original resolve of one who has left the household life, and to betray the profound kindness of those who gave birth and raised us—once fallen into the three miserable realms, one may well pass through ten thousand kalpas. Furthermore, dhyāna-concentration and wisdom take the precepts as their foundation;

bodhi and nirvana take the precepts as their root. When the Way-Loving Goddess (Avalokiteśvara) made her earnest entreaty, it was out of deep compassion for those submerged in samsara, for the Great Awakened One.

Knowing the critical junctures [of human nature], he strictly imposed regulations; for the seeds of karma from beginningless time are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and names manifest according to circumstances—how could they be limited to eighty-four thousand?

He established precepts according to each transgression, codifying three hundred and forty-eight articles as the standard for exposition and the path for maintaining observance and committing violations.
If one has not recited them after five summer retreats, one must remain under the tutelage of a teacher for the rest of one's life.

If one does not hear [the recitation] for half a month, one incurs an offense for violating the teachings; for this reason, I have ventured to re-determine the text for Bhikṣuṇīs based on the monastic precepts.

Where both [versions] are identical, there has been no alteration whatsoever; where that [version] lacks what is present here, it must be examined in detail so that the phrasing and meaning may be harmonious and easy to recite and maintain.
Many among the Bhikṣuṇī community of Siming delight in the precepts; they have joined their efforts and contributed their wealth to carve these into woodblocks.

I wish to propagate this seal widely throughout the world and greatly revitalize the wind of the Vinaya, so that both those within and without may follow it together and cause the Buddha-dharma to abide for a long time.

Come freely and listen to my words: the Unsurpassed Dharma King, the Compassionate Father of Ten Thousand Virtues, has not abandoned you—members of the final age, the base and ordinary stream—but has instead provided detailed instructions on subtle faults and afflictions; this may truly be called a teaching for the rest of one's life.

With hands extended over the ocean of suffering, how can those lost on the path fail to reflect upon their own body and mind, instead giving rise to derisive laughter? Some may harbor shame and remain silent;
others may cover their ears in fear of hearing. How could they know that the establishment of these prohibitions and punishments is entirely due to the deluded karma of one's own mind?

Thus, the *Sudarsana-vibhasa* states: "Regarding this Dharma of the precepts, those who hear its exposition must be careful not to be startled or alarmed, but should instead give rise to a sense of shame and remorse."
Having contemplated the Buddha’s benevolence and virtue, one becomes free from attachment and attains a state of purity. He established the precepts for us and spoke these words of warning:
"If the Buddha had not spoken them, how could they be known? One should carefully examine this text and deeply reproach oneself;
whether reciting or listening, it is fitting to revere and follow it.

This *Bhikṣuṇī-Prātimokṣa-Sūtra*, revised according to the Dharmaguptaka school,
is extracted from that tradition.
I prostrate and pay homage to all Buddhas, As well as to the Dharma and the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus.
Now I shall expound the Vinaya rules so that the True Dharma may long endure. The precepts are like a boundless ocean; Like jewels, one seeks them without satiety.
Desiring to protect the noble wealth of the Dharma, Gathered assembly, listen to my words: I wish to eliminate the eight offenses involving expulsion.
And having extinguished the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas, obstructing the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses—O assembly, listen as I speak:
Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni;
these World-Honored Ones, the Great Virtuous Ones, have explained this matter for my sake.
I now wish to speak well; may all you worthy ones listen together.
Just as a person whose feet are destroyed is unable to travel anywhere, so it is with one who has violated the precepts.
If one wishes to be born among gods or humans, or if one wishes to be born in the heavens, one must always protect the feet of the precepts.
Do not allow it to be damaged, like a driver entering a perilous path; the anxiety over a lost axle-pin or a broken shaft is the same as the anxiety over the destruction of the precepts.
At the time of death, one harbors fear, just as a person looking into a mirror experiences joy or sorrow based on whether they appear beautiful or ugly;
the recitation of the precepts is likewise, for their integrity or destruction gives rise to joy or grief.
As when two armies engage in battle, The brave advance while the timid retreat, So it is with the recitation of the precepts:
From purity comes peace, from defilement comes fear. Among those of the world, the king is supreme; Among all flowing waters, the ocean is supreme;
Among all the stars, the moon is supreme; Among all holy beings, the Buddha is supreme. Among all codes of discipline, [the Vinaya is supreme].
The Sūtra on the Precepts is supreme; the Tathāgata established these prohibitions.

Every half-month, the Saṃgha assembles to recite them. [Question: "Is the Saṃgha assembled? [Answer: "The Saṃgha is assembled. [Question: "Are you in harmony? [Answer: "We are in harmony. [Question: "Let those who have not received full ordination depart.

[If there are such, they are sent away; answer: "Those who have not received full ordination have already departed. [If there are none, say: "There are no here who have not received full ordination. [Question: "Have the bhikṣuṇīs who did not come declared their consent (*chanda*)?"

And regarding the purity (*pārisuddhi*): [If someone says, "I declare my desire and my purity," it is said that the desire and purity have been declared; if there is no one, it is said, "There is no declaration of desire and purity. The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what shall we perform? [The answer is:

"We shall perform the *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the precepts. Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen! Today is the fifteenth day of the waxing moon (or the waning moon, or the fourteenth day, as appropriate according to the season).

The community of monks is to recite the precepts. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, being patient and attentive, grant permission for us to recite the precepts in harmony. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
[Question: "Is the ritual procedure (karmavācanā) accomplished?
[Answer: "It is accomplished. "Sisters, I now wish to recite the Prātimokṣa. All bhikṣuṇīs should assemble in one place;
you must listen attentively and reflect well upon it. If there is anyone who has committed an offense, she should confess it; those without offense should remain silent."
Since they remain silent, it is known that the sisters are pure. If anyone were to question them, they should answer truthfully accordingly.
Thus, if any bhikṣuṇīs among the assembly, having been questioned up to three times, remember an offense but do not confess it, they incur the offense of intentional lying.
The Buddha has declared that intentional lying is a dharma that obstructs the Path. Those bhikṣuṇīs [are thus at fault].
Those who remember having committed an offense and desire to seek purification should perform confession; through confession, there is peace and happiness.
Sisters, I have now recited the introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
I now ask the sisters: Are you pure in this regard? (The heavenly voice says: The sisters are pure in this regard, for they remain silent.

Sisters, these eight *pārājika* dharmas come from the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, which is recited every half-month.
If a bhikṣuṇī, who shares the precepts and dwells together in the precepts, does not relinquish them, nor admits to weakness, and commits an act of impurity, then—

If a bhikṣuṇī, whether in a village or in a secluded place, takes what has not been given with the intent to steal—according to the law regarding taking what is not given—and is subsequently seized by a king or a great minister, or bound, or driven out of the country, or killed, she commits a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion. If she shares this [offense] even with animals, she is a bhikṣuṇī who has committed a pārājika and is no longer in communion.

If a bhikṣuṇī, whether in a village or in a secluded place, takes what has not been given with the intent to steal—according to the law regarding taking what is not given—and is subsequently seized by a king or a great minister, or bound, or driven out of the country, or killed, you [must recognize her as such].
"You are a thief! You are deluded! You know nothing! This bhikṣuṇī has committed a pārājika offense and may not live in communion.
If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally takes the life of a human being—whether by handing a knife to another, praising death as pleasant, encouraging death, saying 'Alas, what is the use of this wretched life?
It would be better to die than to live,' or by reflecting in such ways and employing various means to praise death."
If a bhikṣuṇī, desiring her own pleasure, encourages death, saying, "Death is bliss," this bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.

If a bhikṣuṇī, though having no actual realization, falsely claims for herself: "I have attained the state of a superior person; I have entered the noble state and realized the sublime Dharma; I know it;
I see it"—and later, whether questioned or not, she desires to conceal [this]... [the rest of the sentence follows the standard Pārājika formula].
Out of impurity, she makes this statement: "I truly did not know or see, yet I said I knew and I saw. This is a false and deceptive speech, except in the case of overweening pride;
such a bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a lustful mind, allows a man with a lustful mind to touch her body from below the armpits to above the knees,
this bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a lustful mind, knowing that a man has a lustful mind, consents to him taking her hand, taking hold of her robe,

entering a secluded place, standing together, speaking together, walking together, leaning their bodies against one another, or making an appointment— this bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and is not to live in community.

If a bhikṣuṇī, having committed a pārājika offense like other bhikṣuṇīs, does not disclose it herself, does not inform others, and does not report it to the Saṃgha, and later at another time—whether that bhikṣuṇī has passed away, has been censured by the Saṃgha, has left the religious life, or has joined a non-Buddhist sect—she then says: "I already knew there was such an offense. A bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and is no longer to live in communion.

If a bhikṣuṇī, wishing to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha, employs the means to bring about such a schism and firmly adheres to that practice of causing a schism without relinquishing it, other bhikṣuṇīs should admonish that bhikṣuṇī, saying: "Sister, do not cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha; do not..."
"If you, Sister, persistently refuse to abandon the practice of destroying the harmony of the Saṃgha through skillful means, the Saṃgha should grant you a formal act of reconciliation.
You ought to live in harmony with the Saṃgha, rejoicing and not disputing, studying under the same teacher so that you may be like water and milk mixed together;

thus, within the Buddha-dharma, there will be increase and you shall dwell in peace and happiness. When that bhikṣuṇī, being thus admonished, still persists and does not abandon [her position], that bhikṣuṇī...
She should be admonished three times to relinquish this matter; if she relinquishes it after the third admonition, it is well. If she does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If that bhikṣuṇī has other associates—whether one, two, three, or even countless others—that bhikṣuṇī...
She should say to that bhikṣuṇī: "Sister, do not admonish this bhikṣuṇī.
This bhikṣuṇī speaks according to the Dharma and according to the Vinaya; we delight in what this bhikṣuṇī says and we approve of it.
That bhikṣuṇī should then admonish that [other] bhikṣuṇī, saying: "Sister, do not speak thus, saying that this bhikṣuṇī..."
"Venerable sisters, this bhikṣuṇī speaks according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Vinaya;
what this bhikṣuṇī says we delight in and we approve of. Yet, this bhikṣuṇī does not speak according to the Dharma nor speak according to the Vinaya.
Sisters, do not seek to cause a schism in the Saṃgha. You should desire harmony with the Saṃgha; sisters, be in joyful accord with the Saṃgha."
"Delighting in non-contention and studying under the same teacher, they dwell in harmony like water and milk, thereby increasing their benefit and living in peace within the Buddha-dharma.
When a bhikṣuṇī is thus admonished, if she persists and does not relinquish her position, that bhikṣuṇī should be formally admonished three times to abandon this matter.
If she abandons it after the third admonition, it is well; if she does not abandon it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī resides in dependence upon a village or town and defiles a family while engaging in evil conduct, and this is witnessed and heard by other bhikṣuṇīs, those bhikṣuṇīs should say to that bhikṣuṇī: "Sister, you have defiled a family and engaged in evil conduct;
this has been witnessed and heard by us. You should now depart from this village and no longer remain here. This is what those bhikṣuṇīs should say.
That bhikṣuṇī said, "Sisters, the Saṃgha now possesses favoritism, anger, fear, and delusion;

there are bhikṣuṇīs who have committed such identical offenses, yet some are expelled while others are not. The bhikṣuṇīs admonished her, saying, "Sister, do not speak these words, claiming that the Saṃgha possesses favoritism, anger, fear, and delusion, and that there are bhikṣuṇīs who have committed such identical offenses..."
Among bhikṣuṇīs, there are those who are expelled and those who are not; yet the Saṃgha is neither attached, nor angry, nor afraid, nor deluded.

When that bhikṣuṇī is thus admonished, if she persists and does not relinquish [her conduct], that bhikṣuṇī should be formally admonished up to three times to relinquish this matter. If, after being admonished up to three times, she relinquishes it...

If a bhikṣuṇī is of an evil nature and does not accept the words of others, and when the bhikṣuṇīs have admonished her in accordance with the Dharma regarding the rules of training, she does not accept the admonition but says:
"Sisters, do not speak to me, whether it be good or bad; I too [will not speak to you]. This constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for one who does not relinquish [her behavior].
She does not speak to the elder bhikṣuṇīs about what is good or bad, saying, "Elder sisters, stop; do not admonish me repeatedly.
Those bhikṣuṇīs should admonish that bhikṣuṇī, saying: "Elder sister, do not refuse to accept admonition; you should accept admonition.
Elder sister, when the bhikṣuṇīs admonish you according to the Dharma, you too should admonish the bhikṣuṇīs according to the Dharma."
In this way, the community of the Buddha’s disciples attains increase when they successively exhort, instruct, and cause one another to repent.
When that bhikṣuṇī is thus exhorted, if she persists in her refusal to relinquish [the matter], that bhikṣuṇī should be formally admonished three times to relinquish it.
If she relinquishes it by the third admonition, it is well; if she does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If bhikṣuṇīs live in close association, commit evil deeds together, spread an evil reputation, and conceal their offenses from one another, other bhikṣuṇīs should admonish them, saying:

"Sisters, do not live in close association, commit evil deeds together, spread an evil reputation, or conceal your offenses from one another; by not living in such association, you shall attain [liberation] within the Buddha-dharma."
"To increase her ease and well-being"—when a bhikṣuṇī is thus admonished and yet persists in her refusal to relinquish that matter, she should be formally admonished up to three times to abandon it.
If she abandons it by the third admonition, it is well; if she does not abandon it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If, when the community of bhikṣuṇīs is formally admonishing a bhikṣuṇī, another bhikṣuṇī instructs her, saying:

"You should not live apart; you should live together. I have also seen other bhikṣuṇīs who do not live apart but engage in evil conduct together, causing an evil reputation to spread, and they conceal their offenses from one another. It was out of anger that the Saṃgha instructed you to live apart. That bhikṣuṇī...
The *bhikṣuṇīs* should admonish that *bhikṣuṇī*, saying: "Sister, do not instruct these *bhikṣuṇīs* by saying, 'Do not live separately.
We also see other *bhikṣuṇīs* living together and committing evil deeds, causing an evil reputation to spread, and concealing their offenses from one another.
It was because of anger that the Saṃgha instructed you to live separately; now it is precisely these two *bhikṣuṇīs* who are living together."
If bhikṣuṇīs dwell together, commit evil deeds, spread an evil reputation, and conceal their mutual offenses, there will be no further benefit for them;
rather, if those bhikṣuṇīs dwell separately within the Buddha-dharma, they will find increase, peace, and a comfortable dwelling.

When those bhikṣuṇīs are thus admonished and yet persistently refuse to relinquish that matter, those monks should admonish them up to three times so that they may relinquish it. Even unto the third admonition...
If she relinquishes it, it is well; if she does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and displeasure over even a minor matter, speaks thus: "I renounce the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha;
it is not only these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, who exist, but there are also other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who practice the holy life."
"Venerable sisters, we too may practice the holy life there. That bhikṣuṇī admonished this bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Sister, do not hastily become angry and displeased over a minor matter and speak such words as, 'I renounce the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
It is not only these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, that exist; there are also other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who practice [the holy life]."
"O practitioners of the holy life, we too may practice the holy life under her.

When that bhikṣuṇī has been thus admonished and still persists in her refusal to relinquish [her position], she should be formally admonished three times to relinquish this matter. If she relinquishes it by the third admonition, it is well;
if she does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī delights in quarreling and, after failing to properly remember the matter of a dispute, subsequently speaks out of anger,
saying, "The Saṃgha now has favoritism, has ill will, has fear, and has delusion," that bhikṣuṇī should be admonished by the other bhikṣuṇīs,
who should say to her: "Sister, do not delight in quarreling and, after failing to properly remember the matter of a dispute, subsequently speak out of anger."

"If one makes such a statement as: 'The Saṃgha has attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion, whereas the Saṃgha is without attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion,' when that bhikṣuṇī is thus admonished, if she persists and does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī should be admonished a second time to relinquish this matter;
if she relinquishes it upon the third admonition, it is well; if she does not relinquish it, there is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
Sisters, I have finished reciting the seventeen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules: nine offenses that are committed at once, and the remainder [to be resolved] upon up to three admonitions.
If a bhikṣuṇī commits any one of these rules, she must undergo the *mānatva* penance before both divisions of the Saṃgha for half a month.
Once that bhikṣuṇī has completed the *mānatva* penance, she should be granted the removal of her offense (*abbhāna*). This should be done within the assembly of both Saṃghas;
if there is even one person missing such that the assembly does not consist of forty members, the offense of this bhikṣuṇī cannot be removed.
The bhikṣuṇīs may also censure her; this is the proper occasion.
Now I ask the sisters: "Are you pure in this matter? (Three times. Since the sisters are silent, they are pure in this matter; thus it shall be held.
Venerable sisters, these thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules come from the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, which is recited every half-month.
If a bhikṣuṇī has finished making her robes and the *kaṭhina* period has ended, she may keep an extra robe for ten days; beyond that, [it must be relinquished].
If one accepts a pure gift and keeps it beyond the permitted limit, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī’s robes are finished and the *kaṭhina* robe-season has ended, if she stays overnight in a different location separated from even one of her five robes—
unless there is a formal authorization (*saṃgha-karman*) by the Saṃgha— it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī, having finished her robes and having had the kaṭhina robe suspended, obtains an out-of-season robe and wishes to accept it, she may accept it;
having accepted it, she must quickly have it made into a robe. If it is sufficient, that is well. If it is insufficient, she may keep it for one month in order to complete it.
If she exceeds this period, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī requests a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, except during the remaining times, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The remaining times are: when robes have been seized, lost, burned, or carried away by water; these are the remaining times.
If a bhikṣuṇī has her robes taken away, lost, burned, or carried off by water,
and a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative invites her at will to give her many robes, that bhikṣuṇī should accept them with moderation. If she exceeds this limit,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī, for whom a layman or a householder’s wife has prepared the price for robes,
goes to that householder’s home before having received an invitation and says, "Excellent, householder!
Prepare such a robe and give it to me so that it may be fine," and she obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If two laymen or two wives of laymen provide the price for a robe for a bhikṣuṇī, and that bhikṣuṇī, having not previously received an invitation to choose freely, goes to the houses of those two laymen and says, "Excellent, laymen! Prepare such a robe and give it to me;
let us make it into one robe together for the sake of its beauty," and if she obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This is a *pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣuṇī, or a king, or a high minister, or a brāhmaṇa, or a householder, or a householder’s wife, sends a messenger to deliver the price for a robe to a bhikṣuṇī, and that messenger says to the bhikṣuṇī: "Sister, I am now sending this robe..."
If the price is such that it may be accepted, that bhikṣuṇī says: "I do not need this; it is appropriate for me to receive clothing at the proper time and in a pure manner.
She should then reply to that messenger: "Does the lady have an attendant?
If the bhikṣuṇī says, "Yes—whether a monastery servant or an upāsaka—these are my attendants," the messenger should go to those attendants.
If a person has given the price for robes and it has already been delivered to a nun, [the nun] should say:
"Sister, I have already given the price for the robes to the attendant designated by you; Sister, please know the time and go there, and you shall obtain the robe.
A nun who needs a robe should go to the place of the attendant and, if she obtains the robe after being reminded once, twice, or thrice, that is well.
If she does not obtain the robe, she should stand silently before her for four, five, or six times to prompt her memory;
it is well if she obtains the robe. If she does not obtain the robe and seeks it beyond that number of times, yet obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If she does not obtain the robe, she should either go herself to the place from which it was sent or dispatch a messenger to say: "Previously, you sent a messenger to deliver..."
"If the price for robes is given to a certain bhikṣuṇī, and that bhikṣuṇī does not ultimately receive the robe, you must return it so that it is not lost;
this is the proper time.
If a bhikṣuṇī receives gold, silver, or money with her own hand, or instructs another to take it, or verbally agrees to accept it—[this constitutes an offense].
Nissaggiya Pācittiya: If a bhikṣuṇī engages in various kinds of buying and selling of precious objects, it is a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī engages in various kinds of trade and commerce, it is a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī possesses an almsbowl that has fewer than five patches and is not leaking, yet seeks a new bowl for the sake of its appearance, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

That bhikṣuṇī must go before the Saṃgha and relinquish that bowl; the Saṃgha shall take the lowest-ranking bowl from among them and give it to her to keep until it breaks—this is the proper procedure.
If a bhikṣuṇī herself solicits thread and has a weaver who is not a relative weave it into a robe for her,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a householder or a housewife has a weaver weave a robe for a bhikṣuṇī...
If a bhikṣuṇī, having not previously received an invitation for a self-invitation (pravāraṇā), goes to a weaver and says, "Make this cloth for me;
you should weave it very well, making it wide, long, firm, fine, and even, and I shall give you the price.
If that bhikṣuṇī obtains the cloth—even if it is worth only a single meal—by giving the price for the cloth, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣuṇī first gives a robe to another bhikṣuṇī and later, out of anger, either takes it back herself or causes someone else to take it back, that bhikṣuṇī must return the robe; if she keeps it, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī has an illness, she may keep ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar for up to seven days and consume them;
if she exceeds this period, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣuṇī has less than ten days remaining until the end of the three-month summer retreat, and there is an urgent gift of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*), she should accept it... [up to] ...even until the end of the retreat.
When keeping robes, one should do so for the prescribed period; if one exceeds this, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī knows that an object intended for the Saṃgha is being diverted by another into her own possession, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī, having sought this, seeks that instead, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. If a bhikṣuṇī,
knowing that an item given by a donor for the Sangha has been diverted and used for another purpose,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (as when a donor gives wealth for the Sangha to build a *poṣadha* hall, and the nuns divert it to make five robes).

If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that the object given by a donor was intended for a specific purpose, diverts it for her own use or for the sake of the Saṃgha when it was requested for another purpose, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
(The donor’s gift of wealth was intended to provide food for the resident bhikṣuṇīs for their peace and comfort; the resident bhikṣuṇīs then shared that wealth and clothing among themselves.)
If a bhikṣuṇī diverts material goods given by a donor for one purpose and uses them for another,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense (as when a donor gives wealth to the Ānanda-ni to build a dwelling, but she diverts it to make five robes for herself).
If a bhikṣuṇī takes property offered by a donor for one purpose, but diverts it for another use intended for the Saṃgha, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense requiring forfeiture).
[This refers to when nuns have solicited funds for a dwelling and subsequently divide them among themselves to make five types of robes.]
If a bhikṣuṇī keeps an extra alms bowl without having performed the ritual of formal relinquishment (*niḥsargika-pāyattika*).
If a bhikṣuṇī keeps many fine-colored vessels, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī first promises a sick-bhikṣuṇī a robe but later does not give it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī accepts an out-of-season robe and makes it into an in-season robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣuṇī first exchanges robes with another bhikṣuṇī and later, out of anger, either seizes them herself or causes another to seize them, that bhikṣuṇī must return the robes; if she takes them, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī requests a heavy robe, its value shall not exceed four *dūṣya* lengths of felt; if it exceeds this, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī requests a light robe, its value shall not exceed two and a half *dūṣya* lengths of woolen cloth; if it exceeds this, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
*Pāyattika*. Sisters, I have now recited the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas.
I now ask the sisters: Are you pure in this matter? (Three times. The sisters are pure in this matter, for they remain silent.
Therefore, this matter is to be held thus.
Sisters, these one hundred and seventy-eight *pāyattika* dharmas come from the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, which is recited every half-month.
If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally speaks falsehoods, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī speaks words of disparagement, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī speaks with double-tongued speech, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī sleeps in the same room as a man, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī sleeps in the same room as a woman who has not received the full ordination for more than three nights,
it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī recites the scriptures together with a person who has not received the full ordination, it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣuṇī,
knowing that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a grave offense, speaks of it to a person who has not received the full ordination—
except when authorized by a formal act of the Saṃgha (saṃghakamma)— it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī speaks of a superhuman state (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) to a person who has not received the full ordination (*upasampadā*), saying, "I know this;
I have seen this; I see it as it truly is," it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī teaches the Dharma to a man for more than five or six sentences, except when a woman of intelligence is present, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Ānanda.
If a bhikṣuṇī digs the earth with her own hands or instructs another to dig it, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī destroys a village of spirits, it is a pāyattika."
If a bhikṣuṇī speaks falsely or uses evasive speech to harass the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī reviles or scolds a monastic official (vaiyāvṛtyakara) of the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī takes a rope bed, a wooden bed, bedding, or a sitting mat belonging to the Saṃgha and spreads it out herself in the open air, or instructs another to do so...
If a person spreads bedding and departs without picking it up themselves or instructing another to pick it up,
it is a *pāyattika*. If a bhikṣuṇī, within a monastic dwelling, spreads a communal bed or sitting mat— whether she spreads it herself or instructs another to spread it—
and then sits or lies upon it and subsequently departs without picking it up herself or instructing another to pick it up, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing in advance where another bhikṣuṇī is staying, later comes and forcibly spreads out bedding and lodges there,
thinking, "If she finds it cramped, she will naturally avoid me," and acts upon such a motive for no other reason,
this is improper conduct; it is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger toward another bhikṣuṇī, being displeased with her, personally drags her out of a communal dwelling or instructs another to drag her out, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī sits or lies down upon a rope bed or a wooden bed with detachable legs on an upper story of a dwelling, [it is a pāyattika].
It is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that water contains living creatures, uses it herself to sprinkle mud or grass, or instructs another to do so,
it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī constructs a large dwelling, including its doors, windows, and various decorative fittings, she must direct that the thatching be limited to two or three layers;
if it exceeds this, it is a pāyattika offense.
If a nun accepts more than one meal at a place where food is being distributed, unless she is ill, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If a nun eats apart from the community, except during the remaining times, it is a *pāyattika* offense. The remaining times are: when one is ill, when robes are being distributed, and so forth.
These are the proper occasions: when making robes, when traveling by land, when traveling by boat, and when receiving alms-food from śramaṇas.

If a bhikṣuṇī goes to a donor's house and is earnestly invited to accept cakes, parched grain flour, or cooked rice, and she requires them, she may accept two or three bowls and carry them to the monastery. There, she should distribute them among the other bhikṣuṇīs for them to eat. If a bhikṣu...
If a bhikṣuṇī, being free from illness, accepts more than two or three bowls [of food], it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī eats at an improper time, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī eats leftover food that has been kept overnight, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī places food or medicine in her mouth without having received it [through formal acceptance], except for water and tooth-sticks, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, having already accepted an invitation, goes to another household before or after the meal without informing another bhikṣuṇī, except during other times, it is a pāyattika.
"Other times" refers to the time of illness, the time of making robes, or the time of receiving robes.
This is the proper occasion:
if a bhikṣuṇī sits down by force in a house where food is being served and where there is treasure, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī sits in a secluded place in a house where food is being served and where there is treasure, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī sits alone with a man on open ground, it is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī says to other bhikṣuṇīs, "Sisters, let us go together to the village;
I shall give you food," and that bhikṣuṇī ultimately does not instruct [the others] to give food to this bhikṣuṇī, saying, "Go away, I [will not give]," [it is an offense].

If a nun says, "I do not enjoy sitting or conversing with you; I find it pleasant to sit and converse alone," and for this reason—rather than by any other means—she sends [the donor] away, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a nun is invited to receive medicine for four months, she should accept it provided she is not ill; if she accepts it beyond that limit, except... [exemptions apply].
To accept a regular invitation, a repeated invitation, a partial invitation, or a lifelong invitation constitutes a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī goes to view a military array except when there is a specific reason, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī has a reason to go into an army and stays for more than two nights until the third night,
it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī stays in an encamped army for two or three nights, or observes the military array and battle, or observes...
To travel with an army consisting of elephants and horses constitutes a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī drinks alcohol, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī sports in water, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī tickles another, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī does not accept admonition, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī terrifies another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī bathes once every half-month, she should do so provided she is not ill; if she exceeds this frequency, it is a pāyattika offense except during special times.
The special times are: the heat of the season, the time of illness, the time of labor, the time of wind, the time of rain, and when one has traveled a long distance—these are the special times.
If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, lights a fire on the open ground for the purpose of warming herself— whether lighting it herself or instructing another to light it—
except in cases of specific necessity, it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣuṇī hides the robes,
bowl, sitting mat, or needle case of another bhikṣuṇī— whether hiding them herself or instructing another to do so— [it is a pāyattika].
If a person conceals [an offense], down to even in jest,
it is a *pāyattika*. If a bhikṣuṇī, having received a robe as a pure gift from a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī,
wears it without asking the owner, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī obtains a new robe, she must dye it one of three types of discolored colors: blue, black, or madder.
If a bhikṣuṇī obtains a new robe and does not dye it one of these three discolored colors—blue, black, or madder—and keeps the new robe as it is, it is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally takes the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly drinks or uses water containing living beings, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally harasses another bhikṣuṇī, even for a brief moment so that she is not at ease, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly conceals a grave offense committed by another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a matter of the four types of disputes has been settled in accordance with the Dharma, subsequently raises it again, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that she is traveling with a group of thieves along the same path, even as far as a village, it is a pāyattika.

If a bhikṣuṇī speaks thus: "I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha; engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path," that bhikṣuṇī should be admonished by saying: "Sister, do not speak such words; do not slander [the Dharma]."
"It is unwholesome, World-Honored One, for one to slander the World-Honored One; the World-Honored One does not speak such words.

The World-Honored One has, by means of countless skillful methods, declared that the practice of sexual desire is an obstacle to the Path. When a bhikṣuṇī is thus admonished, if she persists and does not relinquish her position, that bhikṣuṇī should be formally admonished three times to relinquish this matter.
If she relinquishes it upon the third admonition, it is well; if she does not relinquish it, [the formal act of suspension shall proceed].
[If she does so], it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī knows that such a person has not performed the formal act [of renunciation] and, despite such evil and heterodox views being unrenounced, provides them with what they require,
performs legal acts (*karmavācanā*) together with them, stays overnight with them, or converses with them, it is a *pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣuṇī knows that a śrāmaṇerī has spoken thus: "I know that the Dharma taught by the Buddha—that engaging in sexual intercourse—is not an obstacle to the path," that bhikṣuṇī should say to this śrāmaṇerī: "Do not speak such words;
do not slander the World-Honored One. To slander the World-Honored One is unwholesome. The World-Honored One did not say such a thing, śrāmaṇerī."
The Blessed One has, by means of countless skillful methods, taught that engaging in sexual desire is an obstacle to the Dharma.
When a śrāmaṇerikā is thus admonished and yet persists in her refusal to relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī should admonish her up to three times to relinquish this matter.
If she relinquishes it after being admonished up to three times, it is well; if she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī should say to the śrāmaṇerikā: "You yourself..."

From this day forward, you are no longer a disciple of the Buddha; you may not follow other bhikṣuṇīs as other śrāmaṇerīs do, nor may you stay with a mahābhikṣuṇī for two or three nights. You have no such right now; depart, get out, and do not remain here!
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a śrāmaṇerī has been expelled, should keep her as a companion and stay in the same lodging, [she commits an offense].
A *pāyattika*. If a bhikṣuṇī, when another bhikṣuṇī is admonishing her in accordance with the Dharma, speaks thus: "I will not train in this precept now;
only when there is one who possesses wisdom and upholds the Vinaya shall I question and challenge him," she commits a *pāyattika* offense. If she seeks [to avoid training], [it is likewise].
An interpreter should raise this objection:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when the precepts are being recited, speaks thus: 'Sister, what is the use of reciting these trivial rules?
When these rules are recited, they cause people distress and shame, and give rise to doubt,' she commits a pāyattika offense because she disparages the precepts."
If a bhikṣuṇī, when the precepts are being recited, speaks these words: "Sister, I only now know that this is a rule;
this is found within the *Śīlaskandha* (Precept Chapter) of the *Poṣadha* (Half-monthly Recitation of Precepts).
If other bhikṣuṇīs know that this bhikṣuṇī has been sitting through two or three such recitations, let alone more, then that bhikṣuṇī is ignorant and lacks understanding.

If one commits an offense, she should be dealt with according to the law; furthermore, an additional offense of ignorance is added. "Sister, you have gained no benefit and have acquired what is unwholesome.
When the precepts were being recited, you did not attend with a single-minded focus nor listen to the Dharma with an attentive ear. Because of this ignorance, it is a *pāyattika* offense."
If a bhikṣuṇī, after a formal legal act (karmavācanā) has been performed together with others, speaks thus:
"The bhikṣuṇīs give away the property of the Saṃgha according to their personal friendships," it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī rises and departs while the Saṃgha is engaged in a legal proceeding without having given her consent (chanda), it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, having already given her consent (*chanda*), subsequently revokes it, she commits a pāyattika offense. If a bhikṣuṇī,
knowing that other bhikṣuṇīs are quarreling, listens to their words and then reports them to those [involved],
she commits a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and displeasure, strikes another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and displeasure, strikes another bhikṣuṇī with her hand, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and displeasure, slanders another with a groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense,
it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī enters the palace gate while a Kṣatriya king— anointed by water— has not yet emerged from his quarters or has not yet concealed his treasures.
If one crosses the threshold [with such items], it is a *pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣuṇī herself takes hold of, or instructs another to take hold of, treasure or articles adorned with treasure, except within a monastery or a lodging place, it is a *pāyattika*. If she does so within a monastery or a lodging place...
If one holds or causes another to hold a jewel or a jeweled ornament, it should be taken by one who recognizes it;
such is the cause for this, and no other.
If a bhikṣuṇī enters a village at an improper time without having informed another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī makes a rope bed or a wooden bed, the legs should be no higher than eight fingers of the Tathāgata, excluding the portion inserted into the socket;
if she cuts them short and they exceed this limit, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī uses *tūla* cotton to stuff a rope bed, a wooden bed, a bedding mat, or a sitting cushion, it is a [pāyattika].
Pāyattika: If a bhikṣuṇī eats garlic, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī shaves three parts of her body with a razor, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī performs the ritual purification with water using a measure no greater than two finger-joints on each side, if she exceeds this, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī fashions a male organ out of lac, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī slaps another, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, when a bhikṣu is eating and is not ill, provides him with water or a fan without cause, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī begs for raw grain, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī voids excrement or urine upon living grass, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, having used a vessel for excrement or urine at night, does not place it outside the wall during the day to discard its contents, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally goes to watch or listen to music and performances, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī enters a village and stands conversing in a secluded place with a man, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī enters a secluded and concealed place together with a man, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, while in a village street or alleyway, sends her companion away to a distance and stands in a secluded spot whispering with a man, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī enters the house of a layperson and sits down without informing the host and then departs, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī enters the house of a layperson and sits upon a bed without informing the host, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī enters the home of a layperson and, without informing the host, spreads out a seat for herself and stays overnight,
it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣuṇī enters a dark room together with a man, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, without having carefully received her teacher’s words, speaks them to others, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, on account of some minor cause, utters a curse, saying: "If such-and-such happens to me, may I fall into the three evil destinies and not be born within the Buddha-dharma;
if such-and-such happens to you as well, may you also fall into the three evil destinies and not be born [therein]," [it is a pāyattika].
In the Buddha-dharma, this constitutes a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī, while engaged in a quarrel, fails to properly remember the matter of dispute and beats her breast and weeps, it is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī lies down on the same bed with another when she is not ill, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī lies down on the same mat and under the same blanket with another, except at other times, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that she arrived after another who was already residing there, and knowing that the other arrived before her,
recites the sūtras, inquires about their meaning, or instructs them in front of that nun for the purpose of causing her distress, it is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī does not tend to a fellow bhikṣuṇī living with her who is ill, it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣuṇī,
during the initial period of the summer retreat, permits another bhikṣuṇī to place a bed in a room and later,
out of anger, drives her out, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī wanders among the people during any season— spring, summer, or winter— except for other valid reasons,
it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣuṇī does not depart after completing the summer retreat, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī travels through inhabited areas in a border region where there is suspicion or fear, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī travels through inhabited areas within a king’s domain where there is suspicion or fear,
it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī associates with and dwells together with laymen or the sons of laymen, engaging in conduct that is not in accordance with the Dharma, and other bhikṣuṇīs admonish her, saying:
"Sister, do not associate with and dwell together with laymen or the sons of laymen, engaging in conduct that is not in accordance with the Dharma;
Sister, you should dwell separately. If you dwell separately, there will be growth within the Buddha-Dharma."

"For the sake of further peace and happiness, when a bhikṣuṇī is thus admonished and persists in her refusal to relinquish [her position], that bhikṣuṇī should be admonished up to three times to relinquish this matter.
If she relinquishes it by the third admonition, it is well; if she does not relinquish it, it is a pāyattika."
If a bhikṣuṇī goes to view the royal palace, decorated painted halls, gardens, or bathing pools, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī bathes in a river, a spring, or a flowing stream while her body is exposed, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī makes a bathing robe, it must be made according to the prescribed measurement. The measurement herein is:
six spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and two and a half spans in width. If it exceeds these dimensions, it constitutes a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī sews a saṃghāṭī for more than five days— except when she is seeking a saṃghāṭī, when the kaṭhina robes have been issued,
or when the six difficult circumstances have arisen— it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī does not wear her saṃghāṭī for more than five days, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī causes an obstacle when a donor intends to give robes to the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī puts on another’s robe without asking the owner, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī takes a śramaṇa’s robe and gives it to an outsider or a white-robed layperson, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with such an intention, obstructs the Saṃgha from distributing robes according to the Dharma—
fearing that her disciples might not receive them—
it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣuṇī, with such an intention, causes the Saṃgha to be unable to extend the kaṭhina robe at the present time, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intention of obstructing the bhikṣuṇī saṃgha from extending the kaṭhina robe so that the five privileges may be relinquished,

acts in such a way, she commits a pāyattika offense. If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intention of obstructing the bhikṣuṇī saṃgha from extending the kaṭhina robe so that the five privileges may be relinquished,
acts in such a way, she commits a pāyattika offense.
If this bhikṣuṇī tells another bhikṣuṇī, "Please settle this dispute for me," yet does not employ the necessary means to bring it to an end, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī takes food in her own hand and gives it to a layperson or a non-Buddhist, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī acts as a messenger for a layperson, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī spins thread with her own hands, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī enters the interior of a layperson’s house and sits or lies down on a small bed or a large bed, it is a pāyattika.
It is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī goes to the house of a layperson and tells the host to prepare bedding for her to stay overnight, yet does not take her leave before departing the following day, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī recites or practices worldly incantations, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī teaches others to recite or practice worldly incantations, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly confers the full ordination upon a woman who is pregnant, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly confers the full ordination upon a woman who is nursing an infant, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly confers the full ordination upon one who is not yet twenty years of age, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī grants the full ordination to an eighteen-year-old girl who has not completed two years of training in the precepts,
even though she has reached twenty years of age, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī grants full ordination to a girl who has completed eighteen years of age, has undergone two years of training in the precepts,
but has not been granted the six rules, and she is only then twenty years old, it is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī grants the full ordination to a girl of eighteen who has completed two years of training in the precepts and the six rules,
but she is not yet twenty years old and the Saṃgha has not granted its permission, it is a pāyattika offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī ordains a woman who has previously been married and is less than ten years of age, and after she has completed two years of training in the precepts, she is permitted to receive full ordination once she reaches twelve years of age;
if she grants full ordination when she is less than twelve years of age, it is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu, using a small measuring scale, grants the two-year training in the precepts to a woman who has previously married and is twelve years of age,
and confers full ordination upon her without informing the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly confers the full ordination upon a prostitute, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī ordains many disciples but does not instruct them in the two years of training in the precepts, nor takes them into her care through the two methods,
it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī does not follow her preceptor for two years, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī confers the full ordination upon another person without the consent of the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī who has not yet reached twelve years of seniority confers the full ordination upon another, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī who has reached twelve years of seniority confers the full ordination upon another without the consent of the Saṃgha,
it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, when the Saṃgha has not authorized her to confer the full ordination upon another, says, "The Saṃgha possesses favoritism, hatred, fear, and delusion;
they authorize [it] for those they desire and do not authorize it for those they do not desire," she commits a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī confers the full ordination upon a woman whose parents or husband have not given their permission,
it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a woman is distressed by grief or anger due to mutual affection for a man,
grants her the going forth and confers the full ordination upon her, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī says to a śikṣamāṇā, "Renounce this and learn that, and I shall confer the full ordination upon you," yet does not subsequently proceed to confer it, it is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī says to a śikṣamāṇā, "Bring your robe; I shall confer the full ordination upon you," and then does not provide the means for her to receive it, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī confers the full ordination (upasampadā) upon another person before a year has passed [since her own ordination],

it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣuṇī has conferred the basic dharma (mūladharma) upon another person and only after one night has elapsed goes before the community of bhikṣus to confer the full ordination, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, on the day she is to receive instruction, does not go to receive it when she is not ill, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī should go before the community of bhikṣus once every half-month to seek instruction, and does not do so, it is a pāyattika.

When a bhikṣuṇī has completed her summer retreat, she should go before the community of bhikṣus and perform the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*) regarding the three matters of what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
If she does not go, it is an offense of expiation (*pāyattika*).
If a bhikṣuṇī observes the summer retreat (varṣā) in a place where no bhikṣus reside, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that there is a bhikṣu-saṃghārāma, enters it without having announced her presence, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī reviles a bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī delights in quarreling and, being unable to properly recall the matter of the dispute, later becomes angry and displeased and reviles the community of bhikṣuṇīs, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī develops an abscess or ulcer on her body and, without informing the community or others,
has a man break it open or bandage it, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī has previously accepted an invitation and, having already finished her meal, eats again, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī gives rise to a mind of jealousy toward a donor's household, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī applies fragrant substances by rubbing them upon her body, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī smears sesame oil on her body and rubs it in, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī causes another bhikṣuṇī to smear and rub [oil] on her body, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī causes a śikṣamāṇā to massage her body, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī causes a śrāmaṇerī to massage her body, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī causes a laywoman to anoint or massage her body, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī wears a garment that crosses over the thighs, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī keeps articles for women’s adornment, except on account of a specific occasion, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī walks about wearing leather sandals and carrying a parasol, except on account of a specific occasion, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, travels by means of a vehicle except under circumstances of necessity, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī enters a village without wearing the saṃkakṣikā, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī arrives at the house of a layperson toward evening without having been previously invited, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī opens the gate of the saṃghārāma toward evening and departs without informing another bhikṣuṇī,
it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu opens the gate of a saṃghārāma after the sun has set and leaves without having informed [another], it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī neither enters the earlier retreat nor the later retreat, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly confers the full ordination upon a woman who constantly discharges urine, feces, mucus,
or saliva, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly confers the full ordination upon a person with both sexual organs, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly confers the full ordination upon a woman whose two channels are conjoined, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly confers the full ordination upon a person hindered by debt or a person hindered by illness,
it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī learns worldly arts and crafts to support her own livelihood, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī teaches worldly arts and crafts to laypeople, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī who has been expelled does not depart, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī wishes to question a bhikṣu regarding the Dharma but asks without first seeking permission, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another has arrived after her while she was already established there, or knowing that she herself has arrived after the other who was already established there,
and desiring to annoy the other, walks back and forth, stands, sits, or lies down in front of her, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly builds a stūpa (i.e., a funerary monument) within a bhikṣu saṃghārāma, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī sees a newly ordained bhikṣu, she should rise to meet him, pay respectful homage, inquire after his well-being, and invite him to sit;
if she fails to do so except when there is a specific reason, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī sways her body for the sake of appearance as she walks, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī engages in the adornment of women by anointing or rubbing her body with perfumes, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī has a non-Buddhist woman apply fragrant unguents or massage her body, it is a pāyattika.
Sisters, I have now recited the one hundred and seventy-eight pāyattika dharmas.
Now I ask the sisters: Are you pure in this matter? (Three times. Since the sisters are silent, they are pure in this matter; thus it shall be held.
Venerable sisters, these eight *pāṭidesanīya* rules come from the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, which is recited every half-month.
If a bhikṣuṇī who is not ill begs for ghee and eats it, that bhikṣuṇī must confess it before another bhikṣuṇī.
"Venerable Sister, I have committed a censurable offense that should not have been done; I now repent before you, Venerable Sister.
This is called the method of repentance (*deśanā-dharma*).
If a bhikṣuṇī who is not ill begs for oil for food, that bhikṣuṇī should repent before other bhikṣuṇīs.
"Venerable sister, I have committed a censurable offense that ought not to have been done; I now repent before you, venerable sister.
This is called the method of repentance (*deśanā-vinaya*).
If a bhikṣuṇī who is not ill begs for honey as food, that bhikṣuṇī should repent before another bhikṣuṇī.
"Venerable Sister, I have committed a blameworthy offense that ought not to have been done; I now confess this transgression before you, Venerable Sister.
This is called the method of confession (*pratideśanā-dharma*).
If a bhikṣuṇī who is not ill begs for black honey-candies (*kṛṣṇa-śarkarā*) as food, that bhikṣuṇī should [confess] before another bhikṣuṇī.
The nun confesses, saying: "Sister, I have committed a blameworthy act that ought not to have been done; I now confess this to you, Sister.
This is called the method of confession (*deśanā-vinaya*).
If a bhikṣuṇī who is not ill begs for milk as food, that bhikṣuṇī should confess to another bhikṣuṇī.
"Venerable sister, I have committed a censurable offense that ought not to have been done; I now repent before you, venerable sister.
This is called the method of repentance (*deśanā-dharma*).
If a bhikṣuṇī who is not ill begs for curd as food, that bhikṣuṇī should repent before another bhikṣuṇī.
"Venerable Sister, I have committed a blameworthy offense that ought not to have been done; I now repent before you, Venerable Sister.
This is called the method of repentance (*deśanā-dharma*).
If a bhikṣuṇī, being without illness, begs for fish to eat, that bhikṣuṇī should repent before another bhikṣuṇī.
"Venerable Sister, I have committed a blameworthy act that ought not to have been done; I now repent before you, Venerable Sister.
This is called the method of repentance (*deśanā*).
If a bhikṣuṇī who is not ill begs for meat to eat, that bhikṣuṇī should repent before another bhikṣuṇī.
"Venerable Sisters, I have committed a blameworthy offense that ought not to have been done; I now repent before you, Venerable Sisters.
This is called the rite of repentance.
Venerable Sisters, I have already recited the eight *pāṭidesanīya* dharmas."
Now I ask the sisters: "Are you pure in this matter? (Three times. Since the sisters are silent, they are pure in this matter; thus it shall be held.
Venerable sisters, these are the rules of training (śaikṣa-dharma) which come from the recitation of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra every half-month:
"One should train oneself to wear the inner robe neatly;
one should train oneself to wear the five robes neatly."
One should train oneself not to enter the homes of laypeople with one's robe tucked over the shoulders.
One should train oneself not to sit in the homes of laypeople with one's robe tucked over the shoulders.
One should train oneself not to enter the homes of laypeople with the robe wrapped around the neck.
One should train oneself not to sit in the house of a layperson with a cloth wrapped around one's neck.
One should train oneself not to enter the house of a layperson with one's head covered.
One should train oneself not to sit in the house of a layperson with one's head covered.
One should train oneself not to skip over steps when entering the house of a layperson.
One should train oneself not to skip over steps when sitting in the house of a layperson.
One should train oneself not to sit squatting inside the house of a layperson.
One should train oneself not to enter the house of a layperson with hands on the hips.
One should train oneself not to sit in the house of a layperson with hands on the hips.
One should train oneself not to enter the house of a layperson swaying the body.
One should train oneself not to sit in the house of a layperson while swaying the body.
One should train oneself not to enter the house of a layperson with dangling arms.
One should train oneself not to sit in the house of a layperson with dangling arms.
One should train oneself to enter the homes of laypeople with the body well-covered.
One should train oneself to sit in the homes of laypeople with the body well-covered.
One should train oneself not to look left and right while entering the homes of laypeople.
One should train oneself not to look left or right while sitting in the house of a layperson.
One should train oneself to enter the house of a layperson in silence.
One should train oneself to sit in the house of a layperson in silence.
